why: Running now, 25 h from 2026-09-17 19:51. First soak of a machine that actually holds its frame budget, so the number will mean something. Closes PIZERO-33 either way: clean, or with the evidence.
Bit us again today: a keyboard plugged in after boot never enumerates, so every measurement session needs a power cycle. Worst daily-use defect and still the leading freeze suspect after 'emulate'.

A flat-field artefact on an ordinary LCD, with audio islands, narrowed blanking, tearing and encoder seams all ruled out by experiment. Unexplained and visible, which makes it a kit blocker rather than a curiosity.
Do it in the same session as PIZERO-120: both need other screens in front of the board. One answers whether the timing is portable, the other whether the fuzz follows the board or the monitor.
Cheap to re-test now and possibly already fixed: the buzz was measured before we knew the stream was 0.9% short, and that shortfall is now 0.0%. Needs one audible test rather than an investigation.
The first-run experience for anyone handed a kit: a missing ROM shows a black screen with no explanation. Small, self-contained, and it is what makes a kit survivable without you on the phone.

The render rewrite was checked by throwaway programs against 2,304 cases. That should have been a test suite, and the next such change will want one. PIZERO-100 is still a four-line test nobody has written.
The case is critical for the first edition and this is the last known defect in it. Batched with PIZERO-104 and PIZERO-105 into one print, which should close three tickets at once.
Turns vetting from a one-off into something every build repeats. The soak harness it depends on now exists and has proven itself twice, so this is mostly assembly.
Overlay programme starts here once the vetting above is done. The catalogue is the only slice with no rendering or timing risk and is verifiable over serial before anything is drawn.

First of the two affordable CoCo 3 features the PIZERO-111 decision chose. Standalone: the GIME timer's register block is free on a CoCo 2 and the scheduled countdown it needs already exists, so it needs no overlay and no faster 6809.
The palette register file, in the real GIME layout so unmodified CoCo 3 software has a chance. Nearly free at runtime: the blit already does a per-pixel LUT lookup, this makes the table writable.

The look: a VDG-format card blitted through the machine's own path. Cheaper than planned now that the render paths are packed stores, and the product build turned out to be single-buffered, so the Fruit Jam arrangement transfers directly.
The feel: F12, key capture that cannot leak into BASIC, paging, and a pause that keeps HDMI audio streaming rather than feeding it silence.

Decide before building the launch path, not after: cold boot, hot swap, or both on different keys. Fruit Jam is inconsistent with itself here, which is the evidence that leaving it implicit does not work.
Selecting something finally starts it. Blocked on porting coco_machine_reset() from the AMOLED port and on the PIZERO-115 decision, which is why it is last of the four slices.

Palette customisation for the classic 6847 modes, written through PIZERO-85's register file. Part 1 needs nothing new; the editor and per-title .pal profiles wait for the overlay, which is why this sits beside the overlay slices rather than before them.
